content:
Bloomberg reports that bipartisan US senators are pressing Apple CEO Tim Cook to commit by August 21 not to use memory chips from Chinese suppliers ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) and Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC). Here's the full story.

A little background

As Apple seeks ways to navigate the ongoing memory shortage, the company has reportedly been hoping to secure the Trump administration's blessing to source components from CXMT and YMTC — both of which have been designated as Chinese military companies by the US Department of Defense.

Legally, Apple doesn't need US government approval to buy chips from these companies, but doing so without government backing could invite significant political fallout.

As such, Tim Cook told The Wall Street Journal in an interview ahead of Apple's recent price hikes that "everything has to be on the table," adding that "we should look at every source of supply."

In the days that followed, The Wall Street Journal reported that Apple had been seeking government assurances to procure chips from CXMT, while the Financial Times reported that Apple was in talks with YMTC over chip purchases. The FT later further reported that Apple had already been testing CXMT's DRAM chips.

More recent reporting has indicated that Apple's use of Chinese memory chips may extend beyond just the China market, with the company seeking government approval to use components from CXMT and YMTC in products sold in regions outside the US.

The report also detailed how Micron has been lobbying the government to reject Apple's request, on the grounds that allowing Chinese suppliers into Apple's supply chain could undermine domestic US memory production.

This isn't the first time Apple has tried to source memory chips from YMTC. Back in 2022, the company explored using the supplier's components in some iPhones sold in China, but shelved the plan after it drew scrutiny from US lawmakers and ran into tighter export controls.

At the time, Senator Marco Rubio, who serves as vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, accused Apple of "playing with fire," while bipartisan lawmakers warned the deal could pose a national security risk.

Lawmakers press again

Bloomberg reported today that "a group of bipartisan US senators is urging Apple to abandon any move to source chips from blacklisted Chinese semiconductor suppliers [CXMT] and [YMTC], warning the iPhone maker could become dependent on a key component from a nation designated as an adversary by the US."

The senators reportedly view Apple's plans as "short-sighted," arguing the move would "ensure that the world's most valuable consumer electronics company relies on a key supply from a company formally designated by the US government as a Chinese military company."

The lawmakers also raised concerns that other companies could follow Apple's lead, potentially undermining domestic US memory production and planned investments in states including Indiana, Idaho, New York, and Virginia.

They added that any initial measure to confine CXMT memory to China-sold products would likely prove difficult to maintain, since "once a component is qualified by Apple manufacturing, extending its application globally is just a procurement decision away."

Finally, beyond demanding that Apple commit by August 21 to "avoid incorporating CXMT or YMTC memory into its products," the senators are also asking Apple to provide details on any information shared with CXMT during its component qualification process, noting that the transfer of controlled technical data to advanced chipmaking facilities in China may require US Commerce Department authorization.

Apple did not immediately respond to Bloomberg's request for comment.
